Supergroups, topics and the 200-member line
When you need to switch (and why you usually can’t)
Platform · September 26, 2026 · 4 min read · Fast Scheduler team

People pick between channel and group by vibes. Wrong tool costs months: a “channel” run as a group drowns in chat noise; a “group” run as a channel feels like shouting into a wall. Here’s the decision, cleanly.
Channel:
only admins post. Unlimited subscribers. Comments optional via attached group. The broadcast medium.
Group:
everyone posts. Up to 200K members as a supergroup. The conversation medium.
Supergroup:
what a group becomes past 200 members — history for new members, admin tools, slow mode.
Value flows one way: news, curation, deals, teaching.
You want a clean archive — channels are permanent, searchable pages of you.
You care about views-per-post. Channel view counts are the currency of swaps and ads (and the number TGStat/Telemetr publish); groups have no equivalent.
The members’ talk is the product: support, community, networking.
You need rapid back-and-forth (voice chats, live help).
The mature setup is a
channel as the front door
and a
group as the living room

, linked so channel posts appear as comments in the group. The channel keeps the signal high and the archive clean; the group keeps the relationships warm; each feeds the other. Almost every serious Telegram operation runs this pair.
Channel posts can be edited after publishing; group messages can too, but comment threads have no “edit for everyone” culture — treat comments as permanent.
Channels don’t need slow mode; groups do, once active.
Private channels with invite links are the standard for paid access — revoke links via admin tools if they leak.
For the group side, moderation is not optional once you grow:
Combot
is the default (analytics + moderation together),
Rose
is the deep-configuration option,
Shieldy

the lightweight anti-spam gate. For the channel side, consistency is what subscribers actually experience: a scheduler keeps the front door predictable even when the living room is on fire (ControllerBot and
both handle multi-channel setups from one chat).
Channel and group rights are granular and worth five minutes of deliberate configuration. On the channel: give co-admins exactly
post messages
edit messages of others
if they draft, but reserve
delete messages
ban subscribers

for the owner — deletion history is the one thing you can't audit after the fact. On the linked group: moderators get invite-by-link, delete and mute; ban stays with the owner. Two details people miss:
anonymous admin
lets a group admin act under the group's identity rather than their own, and posting
as the channel
inside the discussion group is a toggle any channel admin has — that's how the brand answers comments without exposing which human pressed send.
Plain groups convert to supergroups automatically when they cross 200 members (or when you flip certain settings); there's no downgrade. For larger communities, the feature that changes everything is
topics
(forum mode): the group becomes threads — support, showcase, off-topic, announcements — instead of one river. Discussion groups linked to channels are usually better
without

topics while small (a topic UI adds a click of friction to drive-by comments), but past a few hundred active members, topics are the difference between a community and noise. Pair topics with slow mode of one to five minutes for the general thread during launches — the firehose becomes readable, and quality arguments survive.

There is no convert button in either direction — a channel can't become a group and a group can't become a channel. The honest workarounds: a group that has accidentally outgrown its purpose becomes a channel by creating the channel, pinning a pointer, and letting the old group go quiet (or handing it to the community as the chat annex); a channel that needs conversation doesn't convert — it creates a discussion group and links it. Plan the structure before you grow: the cost of a wrong-shaped container rises with every thousand members, because the audience — not the settings — is what's hard to move.
Common questions
Can a Telegram group have unlimited members?
No — groups cap at 200,000 members when converted to supergroups. Channels have no practical subscriber limit.
Can subscribers reply in a Telegram channel?
Only through comments, which actually live in an attached discussion group. Without one, a channel is read-only.
Can I convert a group into a channel or vice versa?
No. They are different objects in Telegram. You can link them, migrate members manually, or keep both — but no direct conversion exists.
Should a new creator start with a channel or a group?
Start with a channel for reach and add the linked group once real discussion appears. A lonely group reads as dead; a channel with a comment section looks curated.
